---
title: "P2 exercise — Account for water movement"
---

Use paper and a calculator if useful. Allow 50–60 minutes. All numerical
observations are invented teaching examples, not a recovered laboratory dataset.
The [tutorial](index.qmd) defines the terms. Leave with calculations, a pathway
diagram and a short experimental-design critique.

## 1. Predict an initial direction

For each cell calculate Ψ = Ψs + Ψp in MPa. Ignore gravity/matric terms for this
small system. Both cells contact the same external solution at −0.4 MPa.

| Cell | Ψs (MPa) | Ψp (MPa) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| A | −0.8 | +0.2 |
| B | −0.7 | +0.5 |

Predict initial net movement for each cell. Why is its final water content not
determined just by retaining these initial values?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Worked comparison

A has −0.6 MPa, so water initially tends to enter from −0.4 MPa. B has
−0.2 MPa, so water initially tends to leave towards −0.4 MPa. Pressure and
solute concentration can change during movement; these are initial predictions.
:::

## 2. Explain an energy-dependent uptake system

A root-cell proton pump is inhibited while other conditions are initially
unchanged. Predict effects on a proton-coupled nutrient carrier, and distinguish
that from passive water movement through an aquaporin. Your explanation must
name the relevant energy source or gradient. Would every transported ion
necessarily respond identically?

## 3. What did the pot actually lose?

Four individually treated pots lose 24, 27, 22 and 25 g over four hours.
Their leaf areas are 0.10, 0.12, 0.10 and 0.11 m². Unplanted soil controls
under the same conditions lose a mean of 4 g per pot. For a teaching estimate,
subtract 4 g from each loss, then divide by time and leaf area.

Calculate the first pot's rate in g m⁻² h⁻¹. List two assumptions in this
correction. Does leaf-area normalisation guarantee fair physiological comparison?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check the first rate

(24 − 4) / (4 × 0.10) = 50 g m⁻² h⁻¹. The correction assumes comparable
soil evaporation and negligible other mass changes. Covering soils, checking
conditions and documenting uncertainty would improve the interpretation.
:::

## 4. Independent units and water stress

One tray is watered and one tray is kept dry. Each contains ten pots, and
three leaves are measured per plant. Explain why 30 leaf measurements per
condition are not 30 independent applications of the tray-level treatment.
Propose a design that can separate treatment from tray/location effects.
State which conclusions remain possible from the original observations.

## 5. A yellow leaf needs a differential explanation

Older leaves yellow while younger leaves remain green. Suggest a nutrient
remobilisation explanation and two alternatives. Name measurements/controls
that would help distinguish them. Then explain why saline soil can produce
water stress even while remaining visibly wet.

## Completion check

Check every potential sign and unit. A good answer to a water-stress question
connects physics, structure and regulation rather than naming ABA alone.
Try the [self-check](quiz.qmd).
